entries.4cafdc3ec5383ae3a2fce9f5aa677f97485ba223: <div sID="gen11290" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="49" osisID="Ps.49" sID="Ps.49"/> <div eID="gen11290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11291" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11292" type="x-p"/> This psalm is a sermon, and so is the next. In most of the psalms we have the penman praying or praising; in these we have him preaching; and it is our duty, in singing psalms, to teach and admonish ourselves and one another. The scope and design of this discourse is to convince the men of this world of their sin and folly in setting their hearts upon the things of this world, and so to persuade them to seek the things of a better world; as also to comfort the people of God, in reference to their own troubles and the grief that arises from the prosperity of the wicked. I. In the preface he proposes to awaken worldly people out of their security (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.1-Ps.49.3">ver. 1-3</reference>) and to comfort himself and other godly people in a day of distress, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.4-Ps.49.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. II. In the rest of the psalm, 1. He endeavours to convince sinners of their folly in doting upon the wealth of this world, by showing them (1.) That they cannot, with all their wealth, save their friends from death, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.6-Ps.49.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. (2.) They cannot save themselves from death, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">ver. 10</reference>. (3.) They cannot secure to themselves a happiness in this world, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.11-Ps.49.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. Much less, (4.) Can they secure to themselves a happiness in the other world, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">ver. 14</reference>. 2. He endeavours to comfort himself and other good people, (1.) Against the fear of death, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">ver. 15</reference>. (2.) Against the fear of the prospering power of wicked people, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.16-Ps.49.20">ver. 16-20</reference>. In singing this psalm let us receive these instructions, and be wise.
entries.1e810f126202012ff79a3c94945aa84aa5fac948: <div eID="gen11292" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11291" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">A Call to Attention.</title> <div sID="gen11293" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear this, all <hi type="italic">ye</hi> people; give ear, all <hi type="italic">ye</hi> inhabitants of the world: <hi type="super">2</hi> Both low and high, rich and poor, together. <hi type="super">3</hi> My mouth shall speak of wisdom; and the meditation of my heart <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> of understanding. 4 I will incline mine ear to a parable: I will open my dark saying upon the harp. <hi type="super">5</hi> Wherefore should I fear in the days of evil, <hi type="italic">when</hi> the iniquity of my heels shall compass me about? <div eID="gen11293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11294" type="x-p"/> This is the psalmist's preface to his discourse concerning the vanity of the world and its insufficiency to make us happy; and we seldom meet with an introduction more solemn than this is; for there is no truth of more undoubted certainty, nor of greater weight and importance, and the consideration of which will be of more advantage to us. <div eID="gen11294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11295" type="x-p"/> I. He demands the attention of others to that which he was about to say (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.1-Ps.49.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hear this, all you people;</hi> hear it and heed it, hear it and consider it; what is spoken once, hear twice. <hi type="italic">Hear and give ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.62.9">Ps. lxii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.62.11">11</reference>. Not only, "Hear, all you Israelites, and give ear all the inhabitants of Canaan," but, <hi type="italic">Hear, all you people, and give ear, all you inhabitants of the world;</hi> for this doctrine is not peculiar to those that are blessed with divine revelation, but even the light of nature witnesses to it. All men may know, and therefore let all men consider, that their riches will not profit them in the day of death. <hi type="italic">Both low and high,</hi> both <hi type="italic">rich and poor,</hi> must come together, to hear the word of God; let both therefore hear this with application. Let those that are high and rich in the world hear of the vanity of their worldly possessions and not be proud of them, nor secure in the enjoyment of them, but lay them out in doing good, that with them they may make to themselves friends; let those that are poor and low hear this and be content with their little, and not envy those that have abundance. Poor people are as much in danger from an inordinate desire towards the wealth of the world as rich people from an inordinate delight in it. He gives a good reason why his discourse should be regarded (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">My mouth shall speak of wisdom;</hi> what he had to say, 1. Was true and good. It is wisdom and understanding; it will make those wise and intelligent that receive it and submit to it. It is not doubtful but certain, not trivial but weighty, not a matter of nice speculation but of admirable use to guide us in the right way to our great end. 2. It was what he had himself well digested. What his mouth spoke was the <hi type="italic">meditation of his heart</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Ps. xix. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">xlv. 1</reference>); it was what God put into his mind, what he had himself seriously considered, and was fully apprized of the meaning of and convinced of the truth of. That which ministers speak from their own hearts is most likely to reach the hearts of their hearers. <div eID="gen11295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11296" type="x-p"/> II. He engages his own attention (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will incline my ear to a parable.</hi> It is called a <hi type="italic">parable,</hi> not because it is figurative and obscure, but because it is a wise discourse and very instructive. It is the same word that is used concerning Solomon's proverbs. The psalmist will himself incline his ear to it. This intimates, 1. That he was taught it by the Spirit of God and did not speak of himself. Those that undertake to teach others must first learn themselves. 2. That he thought himself nearly concerned in it, and was resolved not to venture his own soul upon that bottom which he dissuaded others from venturing theirs upon. 3. That he would not expect others should attend to that which he himself did not attend to as a matter of the greatest importance. Where God <hi type="italic">gives the tongue of the learned</hi> he first <hi type="italic">wakens the ear to hear as the learned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen11296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11297" type="x-p"/> III. He promises to make the matter as plain and as affecting as he could: <hi type="italic">I will open my dark saying upon the harp.</hi> What he learned for himself he would not conceal or confine to himself, but would communicate, for the benefit of others. 1. Some understood it not, it was a riddle to them; tell them of the vanity of the things that are seen, and of the reality and weight of invisible things, and they say, <hi type="italic">Ah Lord God! doth he not speak parables?</hi> For the sake of such, he would open this dark saying, and make it so plain that he that runs might read it. 2. Others understood it well enough, but they were not moved by it, it never affected them, and for their sake he would open it upon the harp, and try that expedient to work upon them, to win upon them. <hi type="italic">A verse may find him who a sermon flies.</hi> Herbert. <div eID="gen11297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11298" type="x-p"/> IV. He begins with the application of it to himself, and that is the right method in which to treat of divine things. We must first preach to ourselves before we undertake to admonish or instruct others. Before he comes to set down the folly of carnal security (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.6">v. 6</reference>), he here lays down, from his own experience, the benefit and comfort of a holy gracious security, which those enjoy who trust in God, and not in their worldly wealth: <hi type="italic">Wherefore should I fear?</hi> he means, <hi type="italic">Wherefore should I fear their fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.12">Isa. viii. 12</reference>), the fears of worldly people. 1. "Wherefore should I be afraid of them? Wherefore should I fear in the days of trouble and persecution, <hi type="italic">when the iniquity of my heels,</hi> or of my supplanters that endeavour to trip up my heels, <hi type="italic">shall compass me about,</hi> and they shall surround me with their mischievous attempts? Why should I be afraid of those all whose power lies in their wealth, which will not enable them to redeem their friends? I will not fear their power, for it cannot enable them to ruin me." The great men of the world will not appear at all formidable when we consider what little stead their wealth will stand them in. We need not fear their casting us down from our excellency who cannot support themselves in their own excellency. 2. "Wherefore should I be afraid like them?" The days of old age and death are the <hi type="italic">days of evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Eccl. xii. 1</reference>. In the day of judgment <hi type="italic">the iniquity of our heels</hi> (or of our steps, our past sins) will compass us about, will be set in order before us. <hi type="italic">Every work will be brought into judgment, with every secret thing;</hi> and <hi type="italic">every one of us must give account of himself.</hi> In these days worldly wicked people will be afraid; nothing more dreadful to those that have set their hearts upon the world than to think of leaving it; death to them is the king of terrors, because, after death, comes the judgment, when their sins will surround them as so many furies; but wherefore should a good man fear death, who has God with him? <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Ps. 23.4</reference>. When his iniquities compass him about, he sees them all pardoned, his conscience is purified and pacified, and then even in the judgment-day, when the hearts of others fail them for fear, he can lift up his head with joy, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.26">Luke xxi. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.28">28</reference>. Note, The children of God, though ever so poor, are in this truly happy, above the most prosperous of the children of this world, that they are well guarded against the terrors of death and the judgment to come.
entries.44b39fb95cc9daed52a41e9954db0044ce45d033: <div eID="gen11298" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vanity of Worldly Riches; The End of the Wicked.</title> <div sID="gen11299" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches; <hi type="super">7</hi> None <hi type="italic">of them</hi> can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him: <hi type="super">8</hi> (For the redemption of their soul <hi type="italic">is</hi> precious, and it ceaseth for ever:) <hi type="super">9</hi> That he should still live for ever, <hi type="italic">and</hi> not see corruption. <hi type="super">10</hi> For he seeth <hi type="italic">that</hi> wise men die, likewise the fool and the brutish person perish, and leave their wealth to others. <hi type="super">11</hi> Their inward thought <hi type="italic">is, that</hi> their houses <hi type="italic">shall continue</hi> for ever, <hi type="italic">and</hi> their dwelling places to all generations; they call <hi type="italic">their</hi> lands after their own names. 12 Nevertheless man <hi type="italic">being</hi> in honour abideth not: he is like the beasts <hi type="italic">that</hi> perish. <hi type="super">13</hi> This their way <hi type="italic">is</hi> their folly: yet their posterity approve their sayings. Selah. <hi type="super">14</hi> Like sheep they are laid in the grave; death shall feed on them; and the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning; and their beauty shall consume in the grave from their dwelling. <div eID="gen11299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11300" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen11300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11301" type="x-p"/> I. A description of the spirit and way of worldly people, whose portion is in this life, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>. It is taken for granted that they have wealth, and a multitude of riches (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.6">v. 6</reference>), houses and lands of inheritance, which they call their own, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">v. 11</reference>. God often gives abundance of the good things of this world to bad men who live in contempt of him and rebellion against him, by which it appears that they are not the best things in themselves (for then God would give most of them to his best friends), and that they are not the best things for us, for then those would not have so much of them who, being marked for ruin, are to be ripened for it by their prosperity, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Prov. i. 32</reference>. A man may have abundance of the wealth of this world and be made better by it, may thereby have his heart enlarged in love, and thankfulness, and obedience, and may do that good with it which will be fruit abounding to his account; and therefore it is not men's having riches that denominates them worldly, but their setting their hearts upon them as the best things; and so these worldly people are here described. 1. They repose a confidence in their riches: <hi type="italic">They trust in their wealth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.6">v. 6</reference>); they depend upon it as their portion and happiness, and expect that it will secure them from all evil and supply them with all good, and that they need nothing else, no, not God himself. Their gold is their hope (<reference osisRef="Job.31.24">Job xxxi. 24</reference>), and so it becomes their God. Thus our Saviour explains the difficulty of the salvation of rich people (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.24">Mark x. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">How hard is it for those that trust in riches to enter into the kingdom of God!</hi> See <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1 Tim. vi. 17</reference>. 2. They take a pride in their riches: <hi type="italic">They boast themselves in the multitude of them,</hi> as if they were sure tokens of God's favour and certain proofs of their own ingenuity and industry (<hi type="italic">my might, and the power of my hand, have gotten me this wealth</hi>), as if they made them truly great and happy, and more really excellent than their neighbours. They boast that they have all they would have (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Ps. x. 3</reference>) and can set all the world at defiance (<hi type="italic">I sit as a queen, and shall be a lady for ever</hi>); therefore <hi type="italic">they call their lands after their own names,</hi> hoping thereby to perpetuate their memory; and, if their lands do retain the names by which they called them, it is but a poor honour; but they often change their names when they change their owners. 3. They flatter themselves with an expectation of the perpetuity of their worldly possessions (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their inward thought is that their houses shall continue for ever,</hi> and with this thought they please themselves. Are not all thoughts inward? Yes; but it intimates, (1.) That this thought is deeply rooted in their minds, is rolled and revolved there, and carefully lodged in the innermost recesses of their hearts. A godly man has thoughts of the world, but they are his outward thoughts; his inward thought is reserved for God and heavenly things: but a worldly man has only some floating foreign thoughts of the things of God, while his fixed thought, his inward thought, is about the world; that lies nearest his heart, and is upon the throne there. (2.) There it is industriously concealed. They cannot, for shame, say that they expect their houses to continue for ever, but inwardly they think so. If they cannot persuade themselves that they shall continue for ever, yet they are so foolish as to think <hi type="italic">their houses</hi> shall, and their dwelling-places; and suppose they should, what good will that do them when they shall be no longer theirs? But they will not; for the world passes away, and the fashion of it. All things are devoured by the teeth of time. <div eID="gen11301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11302" type="x-p"/> II. A demonstration of their folly herein. In general (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">This their way is their folly.</hi> Note, The way of worldliness is a very foolish way: those that lay up their treasure on earth, and set their affections on things below, act contrary both to right reason and to their true interest. God himself pronounced him <hi type="italic">a fool</hi> who thought his goods were laid up for many years, and that they would be a portion for his soul, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.19-Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 19, 20</reference>. And yet their posterity approve their sayings, agree with them in the same sentiments, say as they say and do as they do, and tread in the steps of their worldliness. Note, The love of the world is a disease that runs in the blood; men have it by kind, till the grace of God cures it. To prove the folly of carnal worldlings he shows, <div eID="gen11302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11303" type="x-p"/> 1. That with all their wealth they cannot save the life of the dearest friend they have in the world, nor purchase a reprieve for him when he is under the arrest of death (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.7-Ps.49.9">v. 7-9</reference>): <hi type="italic">None of them can by any means redeem his brother,</hi> his brother worldling, who would give counter-security out of his own estate, if he would but be bail for him: and gladly he would, in hopes that he might do the same kindness for him another time. But their words will not be taken one for another, nor will one man's estate be the ransom of another man's life. God does not value it; it is of no account with him; and the true value of things is as they stand in his books. His justice will not accept it by way of commutation or equivalent. The Lord of our brother's life is the Lord of our estate, and may take both if he please, without either difficulty to himself or wrong to us; and therefore one cannot be ransom for another. We cannot bribe death, that our brother should still live, much less that he should live for ever, in this world, nor bribe the grave, that he should not see corruption; for we must needs die, and return to the dust, and there is no discharge from that war. What folly is it to trust to that, and boast of that, which will not enable us so much as for one hour to respite the execution of the sentence of death upon a parent, a child, or friend that is to us as our own soul! It is certainly true that <hi type="italic">the redemption of the soul is precious and ceaseth for ever;</hi> that is, life, when it is going, cannot be arrested, and when it is gone it cannot be recalled, by any human art, or worldly price. But this looks further, to the eternal redemption which was to be wrought out by the Messiah, whom the Old-testament saints had an eye to as the Redeemer. Everlasting life is a jewel of too great a value to be purchased by the wealth of this world. We are <hi type="italic">not redeemed with corruptible things, such as silver and gold,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18-1Pet.1.19">1 Pet. i. 18, 19</reference>. The learned Dr. Hammond applies the <reference osisRef="Ps.49.8-Ps.49.9">8th and 9th verses</reference> expressly to Christ: "<hi type="italic">The redemption of the soul shall be precious,</hi> shall be high-prized, it shall cost very dear; but, being once wrought, it shall cease for ever, it shall never need to be repeated, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.25-Heb.9.26">Heb. ix. 25, 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.12">x. 12</reference>. And he (that is, the Redeemer) <hi type="italic">shall yet live for ever, and shall not see corruption;</hi> he shall rise again before he sees corruption, and then shall live for evermore," <reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Rev. i. 18</reference>. Christ did that for us which all the riches of the world could not do; well therefore may he be dearer to us than any worldly things. Christ did that for us which a brother, a friend, could not do for us, no, not one of the best estate or interest; and therefore those that <hi type="italic">love father or brother more than him are not worthy of him.</hi> This likewise shows the folly of worldly people, who sell their souls for that which would never buy them. <div eID="gen11303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11304" type="x-p"/> 2. That with all their wealth they cannot secure themselves from the stroke of death. The worldling sees, and it vexes him to see it, that <hi type="italic">wise men die, likewise the fool and the brutish person perish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">v. 10</reference>. Therefore he cannot but expect that it will, at length, come to his own turn; he cannot find any encouragement to hope that he himself shall continue for ever, and therefore foolishly comforts himself with this, that, though he shall not, his house shall. Some rich people are wise, they are politicians, but they cannot out-wit death, nor evade his stroke, with all their art and management; others are fools and brutish (<hi type="italic">Fortuna favet fatuis—Fools are Fortune's favourites</hi>); these, though they do no good, yet perhaps do no great hurt in the world: but that shall not excuse them; they shall perish, and be taken away by death, as well as the wise that did mischief with their craft. Or by the wise and the foolish we may understand the godly and the wicked; the godly die, and their death is their deliverance; the wicked perish, and their death is their destruction; but, however, they leave their wealth to others. (1.) They cannot continue with it, nor will it serve to procure them a reprieve. That is a frivolous plea, though once it served a turn (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.8">Jer. xli. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Slay us not, for we have treasures in the field.</hi> (2.) They cannot carry it away with them, but must leave it behind them. (3.) They cannot foresee who will enjoy it when they have left it; they must leave it to others, but to whom they know not, perhaps to a fool (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.19">Eccl. ii. 19</reference>), perhaps to an enemy. <div eID="gen11304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11305" type="x-p"/> 3. That, as their wealth will stand them in no stead in a dying hour, so neither will their honour (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Man, being in honour, abides not.</hi> We will suppose a man advanced to the highest pinnacle of preferment, as great and happy as the world can make him, man in splendour, man at his best estate, surrounded and supported with all the advantages he can desire; yet then he abides not. His honour does not continue; that is a fleeting shadow. He himself does not, he tarries not all night; this world is an inn, in which his stay is so short that he can scarcely be said to get a night's lodging in it; so little rest is there in these things; he has but a baiting time. <hi type="italic">He is like the beasts that perish;</hi> that is, he must as certainly die as the beasts, and his death will be as final a period to his state in this world as theirs is; his dead body likewise will putrefy as theirs does; and (as Dr. Hammond observes) frequently the greatest honours and wealth, unjustly gotten by the parent, descend not to any one of his posterity (as the beasts, when they die, leave nothing behind them to their young ones, but the wide world to feed in), but fall into other hands immediately, for which he never designed to gather them. <div eID="gen11305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11306" type="x-p"/> 4. That their condition on the other side of death will be very miserable. The world they dote upon will not only not save them from death, but will sink them so much the lower into hell (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Like sheep they are laid in the grave.</hi> Their prosperity did but feed them like sheep for the slaughter (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.16">Hos. iv. 16</reference>), and then death comes, and shuts them up in the grave like fat sheep in a fold, <hi type="italic">to be brought forth to the day of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.30">Job xxi. 30</reference>. Multitudes of them, like flocks of sheep dead of some disease, are thrown into the grave, and there death shall feed on them, the second death, <hi type="italic">the worm that dies not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.24.20">Job xxiv. 20</reference>. Their own guilty consciences, like so many vultures, shall be continually preying upon them, with, <hi type="italic">Son, remember,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>. Death insults and triumphs over them, as it is represented in the fall of the king of Babylon, at which <hi type="italic">hell from beneath is moved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9-Isa.14.23">Isa. xiv. 9</reference>, &c. While a saint can ask proud Death, <hi type="italic">Where is thy sting?</hi> Death will ask the proud sinner, <hi type="italic">Where is thy wealth, thy pomp?</hi> and the more he was fattened with prosperity the more sweetly will death feed on him. And in the morning of the resurrection, when all that sleep in the dust shall awake (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">the upright shall have dominion over them,</hi> shall not only be advanced to the highest dignity and honour when they are filled with everlasting shame and contempt, elevated to the highest heavens when they are sunk to the lowest hell, but they shall be assessors with Christ in passing judgment upon them, and shall applaud the justice of God in their ruin. When the rich man in hell begged that Lazarus might bring him a drop of water to cool his tongue he owned that that upright man had dominion over him, as the foolish virgins also owned the dominion of the wise, and that they lay much at their mercy, when they begged, <hi type="italic">Give us of your oil.</hi> Let this comfort us in reference to the oppressions which the upright are now often groaning under, and the dominion which the wicked have over them. The day is coming when the tables will be turned (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.1">Esther ix. 1</reference>) and the upright will have the dominion. Let us now judge of things as they will appear at that day. But what will become of all the beauty of the wicked? Alas! that shall all be <hi type="italic">consumed in the grave from their dwelling;</hi> all that upon which they valued themselves, and for which others caressed and admired them, was adventitious and borrowed; it was paint and varnish, and they will rise in their own native deformity. The beauty of holiness is that which the grave, that consumes all other beauty, cannot touch, or do any damage to. Their beauty shall consume, the grave (or hell) being a habitation to every one of them; and what beauty can be there where there is nothing but the blackness of darkness for ever?
entries.03fdebc1ec0385e4499d9abdf8925444f0fae177: <div eID="gen11306" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Privilege of the Godly.</title> <div sID="gen11307" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> But God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave: for he shall receive me. Selah. <hi type="super">16</hi> Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased; <hi type="super">17</hi> For when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him. <hi type="super">18</hi> Though while he lived he blessed his soul: and <hi type="italic">men</hi> will praise thee, when thou doest well to thyself. <hi type="super">19</hi> He shall go to the generation of his fathers; they shall never see light. <hi type="super">20</hi> Man <hi type="italic">that is</hi> in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts <hi type="italic">that</hi> perish. <div eID="gen11307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11308" type="x-p"/> Good reason is here given to good people, <div eID="gen11308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11309" type="x-p"/> I. Why they should not be afraid of death. There is no cause for that fear if they have such a comfortable prospect as David here has of a happy state on the other side death, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">v. 15</reference>. He had shown (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">v. 14</reference>) how miserable the dead are that die in their sins, where he shows how blessed the dead are that die in the Lord. The distinction of men's outward condition, how great a difference soever it makes in life, makes none at death; rich and poor meet in the grave. But the distinction of men's spiritual state, though, in this life, it makes a small difference, where all things come alike to all, yet, at and after death, it makes a very great one. <hi type="italic">Now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.</hi> The righteous has hope in his death, so has David here hope in God concerning his soul. Note, The believing hopes of the soul's redemption from the grave, and reception to glory, are the great support and joy of the children of God in a dying hour. They hope, <div eID="gen11309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11310" type="x-p"/> I. That God will redeem their souls from the power of the grave, which includes, (1.) The preserving of the soul from going to the grave with the body. The grave has a power over the body, by virtue of the sentence (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Gen. iii. 19</reference>), and it is cruel enough in executing that power (<reference osisRef="Song.8.6">Cant. viii. 6</reference>); but is has no such power over the soul. It has power to silence, and imprison, and consume the body; but the soul then moves, and acts, and converses, more freely than ever (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.9-Rev.6.10">Rev. vi. 9, 10</reference>); it is immaterial and immortal. When death breaks the dark lantern, yet it does not extinguish the candle that was pent up in it. (2.) The reuniting of the soul and body at the resurrection. The soul is often put for the life; that indeed falls under the power of the grave for a time, but it shall, at length, be redeemed from it, when <hi type="italic">mortality shall be swallowed up of life.</hi> The God of life, that was its Creator at first, can and will be its Redeemer at last. (3.) The salvation of the soul from eternal ruin: "<hi type="italic">God shall redeem my soul from the sheol of hell</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">v. 15</reference>), the wrath to come, that pit of destruction into which the wicked shall be cast," <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">v. 14</reference>. It is a great comfort to dying saints that they shall not be hurt of the second death (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.11">Rev. ii. 11</reference>), and therefore the first death has no sting and the grave no victory. <div eID="gen11310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11311" type="x-p"/> 2. That he will receive them to himself. He redeems their souls, that he may receive them. <reference osisRef="Ps.31.5">Ps. xxxi. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">Into thy hands I commit my spirit, for thou has redeemed it.</hi> He will receive them into his favour, will admit them into his kingdom, into the mansions that he prepared for them (<reference osisRef="John.14.2-John.14.3">John xiv. 2, 3</reference>), those everlasting habitations, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.9">Luke xvi. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen11311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11312" type="x-p"/> II. Why they should not be afraid of the prosperity and power of wicked people in this world, which, as it is their pride and joy, has often been the envy, and grief, and terror of the righteous, which yet, all things considered, there is no reason for. <div eID="gen11312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11313" type="x-p"/> 1. He supposes the temptation very strong to envy the prosperity of sinners, and to be afraid that they will carry all before them with a high hand, that with their wealth and interest they will run down religion and religious people, and that they will be found the truly happy people; for he supposes, (1.) That they are made rich, and so are enabled to give law to all about them and have every thing at command. <hi type="italic">Pecuniæ obediunt omnes et omnia—Every person and every thing obey the commanding influence of money.</hi> (2.) That the glory of their house, from very small beginnings, is increased greatly, which naturally makes men haughty, insolent, and imperious, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.16">Ps. v. 16</reference>. Thus they seem to be the favourites of heaven, and therefore formidable. (3.) That they are very easy and secure in themselves and in their own minds (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">In his life-time he blessed his soul;</hi> that is, he thought himself a very happy man, such a one as he would be, and a very good man, such a one as he should be, because he prospered in the world. He blessed his soul, as that rich fool who said to his soul, "<hi type="italic">Soul, take thy ease,</hi> and be not disturbed either with cares and fears about the world or with the rebukes and admonitions of conscience. All is well, and will be well for ever." Note, [1.] It is of great consequence to consider what that is in which we bless our souls, upon the score of which we think well of ourselves. Believers <hi type="italic">bless themselves in the God of truth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.16">Isa. lxv. 16</reference>) and think themselves happy if he be theirs; carnal people bless themselves in the wealth of the world, and think themselves happy if they have abundance of that. [2.] There are many whose precious souls lie under God's curse, and yet they do themselves bless them; they applaud that in themselves which God condemns, and speak peace to themselves when God denounces war against them. Yet this is not all. (4.) They are in good reputation among their neighbours: "<hi type="italic">Men will praise thee,</hi> and cry thee up, as having done well for thyself in raising such an estate and family." This is the sentiment of all the children of this world, that those do best for themselves that do most for their bodies, by heaping up riches, though, at the same time, nothing is done for the soul, nothing for eternity; and accordingly they <hi type="italic">bless the covetous, whom the Lord abhors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Ps. x. 3</reference>. If men were to be our judges, it were our wisdom thus to recommend ourselves to their good opinion: but what will it avail us to be approved of men if God condemn us? Dr. Hammond understands this of the good man here spoken to, for it is the second person, not of the wicked man spoken of: "<hi type="italic">He, in his life-time, blessed his soul, but thou shalt be praised for doing well unto thyself.</hi> The worldling magnified himself; but thou that dost not, like him, speak well of thyself, but do well for thyself, in securing thy eternal welfare, thou shalt be praised, if not of men, yet of God, which will be thy everlasting honour." <div eID="gen11313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11314" type="x-p"/> 2. He suggests that which is sufficient to take off the strength of the temptation, by directing us to look forward to the end of prosperous sinners (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>): "Think what they will be in the other world, and you will see no cause to envy them what they are and have in this world." <div eID="gen11314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11315" type="x-p"/> (1.) In the other world they will be never the better for all the wealth and prosperity they are now so fond of. It is a miserable portion, which will not last so long as they must (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">When he dies</hi> it is taken for granted that he goes into another world himself, but <hi type="italic">he shall carry nothing away with him</hi> of all that which he has been so long heaping up. The greatest and wealthiest cannot therefore be the happiest, because they are never the better for their living in this world; as they came naked into it, they shall go naked out of it. But those have something to show in the other world for their living in this world who can say, through grace, that though they came corrupt, and sinful, and spiritually naked, into it, they go renewed, and sanctified, and well clothed with the righteousness of Christ, out of it. Those that are rich in the graces and comforts of the Spirit have something which, when they die, they shall carry away with them, something which death cannot strip them of, nay, which death will be the improvement of; but, as for worldly possessions, as we <hi type="italic">brought nothing into the world</hi> (what we have we had from others), so it is certain that we shall carry nothing out, but leave it to others, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.7">1 Tim. vi. 7</reference>. They shall descend, but <hi type="italic">their glory,</hi> that which they called and counted their glory, and gloried in, <hi type="italic">shall not descend after them</hi> to lessen the disgrace of death and the grave, to bring them off in the judgment, or abate the torments of hell. Grace is glory that will ascend with us, but no earthly glory will descend after us. <div eID="gen11315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11316" type="x-p"/> (2.) In the other world they will be infinitely the worse for all their abuses of the wealth and prosperity they enjoyed in this world (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The soul shall go to the generation of his fathers,</hi> his worldly wicked fathers, whose sayings he approved and whose steps he trod in, his fathers who would not hearken to the word of God, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.4">Zech. i. 4</reference>. He shall go to be there where they are that shall never see light, shall never have the least glimpse of comfort and joy, being condemned to utter darkness. Be not afraid then of the pomp and power of wicked people; for the end of the man that is in honour, if he be not wise and good, will be miserable; if he understand not, he is to be pitied rather than envied. A fool, a wicked man, in honour, is really as despicable an animal as any under the sun; he is <hi type="italic">like the beasts that perish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.20">v. 20</reference>); nay, it is better to be a beast than to be a man that makes himself like a beast. Men in honour that understand, that know and do their duty and make conscience of it, are as gods, and children of the Most High. But men in honour that understand not, that are proud, and sensual, and oppressive, are as beasts, and they shall perish, like the beasts, ingloriously as to this world, though not, like the beasts, indemnified as to another world. Let prosperous sinners therefore be afraid for themselves, but let not even suffering saints be afraid of them.  <chapter eID="Ps.49"/> <div eID="gen11316" type="x-p"/>

entries.0c6da36352448b5c4ebd0445674152791f799f46: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6027"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 49</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.49.1-Ps.49.20">Psa 49:1-20</reference>. This Psalm instructs and consoles. It teaches that earthly advantages are not reliable for permanent happiness, and that, however prosperous worldly men may be for a time, their ultimate destiny is ruin, while the pious are safe in God's care.</title> <div sID="gen9190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6027"/>1-3. All are called to hear what interests all.<div eID="gen9190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">world--</hi>literally, "duration of life," the present time. <div eID="gen9191" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ed9794eecd15b8bd75b58207c814fa4fca6446e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6028"/><div sID="gen9192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6028"/><hi type="bold">4. incline--</hi>to hear attentively (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.6">Psa 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">31:2</reference>).<div eID="gen9192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">parable--</hi>In Hebrew and Greek "parable" and "proverb" are translations of the same word. It denotes a comparison, or form of speech, which under one image includes many, and is expressive of a general truth capable of various illustrations. Hence it may be used for the illustration itself. For the former sense, "proverb" (that is, one word for several) is the usual English term, and for the latter, in which comparison is prominent, "parable" (that is, one thing laid by another). The distinction is not always observed, since here, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.2">Psa 78:2</reference>; "proverb" would better express the style of the composition (compare also <reference osisRef="Prov.26.7">Pr 26:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Ha 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.25">Joh 16:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.16.29">29</reference>). Such forms of speech are often very figurative and also obscure (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.13.12-Matt.13.15">Mt 13:12-15</reference>). Hence the use of the parallel word--<div eID="gen9193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dark saying--</hi>or, "riddle" (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.2">Eze 17:2</reference>).<div eID="gen9194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">open--</hi>is to explain.<div eID="gen9195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the harp--</hi>the accompaniment for a lyric. <div eID="gen9196" type="x-p"/>
entries.64bf8d925cd57dcda9237f0b10cb0c4369f5d071: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6029"/><div sID="gen9197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6029"/><hi type="bold">5. iniquity--</hi>or, "calamity" (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">Psa 40:12</reference>).<div eID="gen9197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of my heels--</hi>literally "my supplanters" (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.36">Ge 27:36</reference>), or oppressors: "I am surrounded by the evils they inflict." <div eID="gen9198" type="x-p"/>
entries.64c259dfcdcf05b3011684eac00129923a78a191: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6030"/><div sID="gen9199" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6030"/>6. They are vainglorious. <div eID="gen9199" type="x-p"/>
entries.21a802140e7a6b041b3e461d85eef75906abb125: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6031"/><div sID="gen9200" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6031"/>7-9. yet unable to save themselves or others. <div eID="gen9200" type="x-p"/>
entries.623114faf5acef3e4b09743c1eea487bc8be5166: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6034"/><div sID="gen9203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6034"/><hi type="bold">10. For he seeth--</hi>that is, corruption; then follows the illustration.<div eID="gen9203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wise ... fool--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Pr 1:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1">10:1</reference>).<div eID="gen9204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">likewise--</hi>alike altogether--(<reference osisRef="Ps.4.8">Psa 4:8</reference>)--die--all meet the same fate. <div eID="gen9205" type="x-p"/>
entries.031584f36dabb03eed76c88fbb1d5e7681328009: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6035"/><div sID="gen9206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6035"/>11. Still infatuated and flattered with hopes of perpetuity, they call their lands, or "celebrate their names on account of (their) lands." <div eID="gen9206" type="x-p"/>
entries.4980b96cb070f627d86668c8f2c80f029cd22092: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6036"/><div sID="gen9207" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6036"/>12. Contrasted with this vanity is their frailty. However honored, man<div eID="gen9207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abideth not--</hi>literally, "lodgeth not," remains not till morning, but suddenly perishes as (wild) beasts, whose lives are taken without warning. <div eID="gen9208" type="x-p"/>
entries.51bf90d3dce73fa65dcd7cf9bf0d255b02312f99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6037"/><div sID="gen9209" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6037"/>13. Though their way is folly, others follow the same course of life. <div eID="gen9209" type="x-p"/>
entries.586e458c9a347d447ce12cb82d705ef026512295: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6038"/><div sID="gen9210" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6038"/><hi type="bold">14. Like sheep--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.49.12">Psa 49:12</reference>) unwittingly, they<div eID="gen9210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are laid--</hi>or, "put," &c.<div eID="gen9211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">death shall feed on--</hi>or, better, "shall rule"<div eID="gen9212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them--</hi>as a shepherd (compare "feed," <reference osisRef="Ps.28.9">Psa 28:9</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen9213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have dominion over--</hi>or, "subdue"<div eID="gen9214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them in the morning--</hi>suddenly, or in their turn.<div eID="gen9215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their beauty--</hi>literally, "form" or shape.<div eID="gen9216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall consume--</hi>literally, "is for the consumption," that is, of the grave.<div eID="gen9217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from their dwelling--</hi>literally, "from their home (they go) to it," that is, the grave. <div eID="gen9218" type="x-p"/>
entries.982a29f68064ab0812369f51acec2d9d683f714b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6039"/><div sID="gen9219" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6039"/>15. The pious, delivered from "the power of the grave."<div eID="gen9219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9220" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">power--</hi>literally, "the hand," of death, are taken under God's care. <div eID="gen9220" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c67f5b2fadb12b05dbcffb2369fcf00617a8c28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6040"/><div sID="gen9221" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6040"/>16-19. applies this instruction. Be not anxious (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.1">Psa 37:1</reference>, &c.), since death cuts off the prosperous wicked whom you dread. <div eID="gen9221" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7549696078d4b7f6db51a5c49d06c917879777f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6042"/><div sID="gen9224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6042"/>20. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.49.12">Psa 49:12</reference>). The folly is more distinctly expressed by "understandeth not," substituted for "abideth not." <chapter eID="Ps.49"/>

entries.98292d2c345dba3aab1876df459e8621ef2f5811: <div eID="gen20179" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20180" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20181" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20181" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20180" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20182" type="x-p"/> All men are invited to attend to lessons of wisdom relative to the insufficiency of earthly good to save or prolong life; to secure the resurrection from the dead, <reference osisRef="Psa.49.1-Psa.49.9">Psa 49:1-9</reference>. Death is inevitable, <reference osisRef="Psa.49.10">Psa 49:10</reference>. The vain expectations of rich men, <reference osisRef="Psa.49.11-Psa.49.13">Psa 49:11-13</reference>. Death renders all alike, <reference osisRef="Psa.49.14">Psa 49:14</reference>. The psalmist encourages and fortifies himself against envying the apparently prosperous state of the wicked, who are brutish, and die like beasts, <reference osisRef="Psa.49.15-Psa.49.20">Psa 49:15-20</reference>. <div eID="gen20182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20183" type="x-p"/> The title, To the chief Musician, A Psalm for the sons of Korah, has nothing particular in it; and the Versions say little about it. One of the descendants of the children of Korah might have been the author of it; but when or on what occasion it was made, cannot now be discovered. The author aimed to be obscure, and has succeeded; for it is very difficult to make out his meaning. It is so much in the style of the Book of Job, that one might believe they had the same author; and that this Psalm might have made originally a part of that book. "It seems," says Dr. Dodd, "to be a meditation on the vanity of riches, and the usual haughtiness of those who possess them. As a remedy for this, he sets before them the near prospect of death, from which no riches can save, in which no riches can avail. The author considers the subject he is treating as a kind of wisdom concealed from the world; a mystery, an occult science with respect to the generality of mankind." Dr. Kennicott has given an excellent translation of this Psalm which is very literal, simple, and elegant; and by it the reader will be convinced that a good translation of a difficult passage is often better than a comment. <div eID="gen20183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20184" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20185" type="x-p"/> Hear this, all ye people - The four first verses contain the author's exordium or introduction, delivered in a very pompous style and promising the deepest lessons of wisdom and instruction. But what was rare then is common-place now.
entries.00e74ad1538b6fabd89c537a8cb91d2ef59cb1af: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20186" type="x-p"/> I will incline mine ear to a parable - This was the general method of conveying instruction among the Asiatics. They used much figure and metaphor to induce the reader to study deeply in order to find out the meaning. This had its use; it obliged men to think and reflect deeply; and thus in some measure taught them the use, government, and management of their minds. <div eID="gen20186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20187" type="x-p"/> My dark saying upon the harp - Music was sometimes used to soothe the animal spirits, and thus prepare the mind for the prophetic influx.
entries.8db9df3c1b6bf554b77e45da834ebdea1f16bb09: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20188" type="x-p"/> The iniquity of my heels - Perhaps עקבי akebai, which we translate my heels, should be considered the contracted plural of עקבים akebim, supplanters. The verse would then read thus: "Wherefore should I fear in the days of evil, though the iniquity of my supplanters should compass me about." The Syriac and Arabic have taken a similar view of the passage: "Why should I fear in the evil day, when the iniquity of my enemies compasses me about." And so Dr. Kennicott translates it.
entries.278662a4bf946c8c753c09f68fe173c7da17bd21: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20189" type="x-p"/> Sone of them can by any means redeem his brother - Wealth cannot save from death; brother, however rich, cannot save his brother; nor will God accept riches as a ransom for the life or soul of any transgressor. To procure health of body, peace of mind, redemption from death, and eternal glory, riches are sought for and applied in vain.
entries.778a64377e94acc51814dbf64fdebc04a0cc8f30: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20190" type="x-p"/> For the redemption of their soul is precious - It is of too high a price to be redeemed with corruptible things, such as silver or gold, and has required the sacrificial death of Christ. <div eID="gen20190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20191" type="x-p"/> And it ceaseth for ever - This is very obscure, and may apply to the ransom which riches could produce. That ransom must be for ever unavailable, because of the value of the soul. Or this clause should be added to the following verse, and read thus: "And though he cease to be, (וחדל vechadal), during the hidden time, (לעולם leolam); yet he shall live on through eternity, (ויחי עוד לנצח vichi od lanetsach), and not see corruption." This is probably the dark saying which it was the design of the author to utter in a parable, and leave it to the ingenuity of posterity to find it out. The verb חדל chadal signifies a cessation of being or action, and עולם olam often signifies hidden time, that which is not defined, and the end of which is not ascertained, though it is frequently used to express endless duration. This translation requires no alteration of the original text, and conveys a precise and consistent meaning.
entries.d3fce66a6e68d447c3bf52e3615b39c6497a0749: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20192" type="x-p"/> For he seeth that wise men die - Though they may be rich, and their wisdom teach them the best method of managing their riches so as to derive all the good from them they can possibly produce, yet they die as well as the fool and the poor ignorant man; and their wealth is left to others who will be equally disappointed in their expectation from it.
entries.dcda96029093c38b75a77ed618429f59c41de18f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen20192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20193" type="x-p"/> Their inward thought is, that their houses shall continue for ever - Thus, by interpolation, we have endeavored to patch up a sense to this clause. Instead of קרבם kirbam, their inward part, the Septuagint appear to have used a copy in which the second and third letters have been transposed קברם kibram, their sepulchres; for they translate: Και οἱ ταφοι αυτων οικιαι αυτων εις τον αιωνα· "For their graves are their dwellings for ever." So six or seven feet long, and two or three wide, is sufficient to hold the greatest conqueror in the universe! What a small house for the quondam possessor of numerous palaces and potent kingdoms! <div eID="gen20193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20194" type="x-p"/> They call their lands after their own names - There would have been no evil in this if it had not been done on an infidel principle. They expected no state but the present; and if they could not continue themselves, yet they took as much pains as possible to perpetuate their memorial.
entries.3f8b5b636aca385d366755188260bc069b8c49e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20195" type="x-p"/> Man being in honor abideth not - However rich, wise, or honorable, they must die; and if they die not with a sure hope of eternal life, they die like beasts. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.49.20">Psa 49:20</reference> (note).
entries.f9067f5cdd981dc6a5ffbcf450f745a14b9d9edd: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen20195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20196" type="x-p"/> Their posterity approve their sayinys - Go the same way; adopt their maxims.
entries.95b0773430110645685616de9820a7489bac5c00: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20197" type="x-p"/> Like sheep they are laid in the grave - לשאול lishol, into sheol, the place of separate spirits. <div eID="gen20197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20198" type="x-p"/> Death shall feed on them מות ירעם maveth yirem, "Death shall feed them!" What an astonishing change! All the good things of life were once their portion, and they lived only to eat and drink; and now they live in sheol, and Death himself feeds them? and with what? Damnation. Houbigant reads the verse thus: "Like sheep they shall be laid in the place of the dead; death shall feed on them; their morning shepherds rule over them; and their flesh is to be consumed. Destruction is to them in their folds."
entries.ccdd8d578df04f2c31ca64b626efea0f24100b11: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen20198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20199" type="x-p"/> But God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave - מיד שאול miyad sheol, "from the hand of sheol." That is, by the plainest construction, I shall have a resurrection from the dead, and an entrance into his glory; and death shall have no dominion over me.
entries.3ecc2c69d99c6d5ccaf77f9f6d84bbacb89a2bf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20200" type="x-p"/> Be not thou afraid when one is made rich - Do not be envious; do not grieve: it will do you no harm; it will do him no good. All he gets will be left behind; he can carry nothing with him. Even his glory must stay behind; he shall mingle with the common earth.
entries.a2135a00184b27c19c495d65fcf7c267d162fedb: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen20200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20201" type="x-p"/> He blessed his soul - He did all he could to procure himself animal gratifications, and he was applauded for it; for it is the custom of the world to praise them who pay most attention to their secular interest; and he who attends most to the concerns of his soul is deemed weak and foolish, and is often persecuted by an ungodly world.
entries.493e4a7a2eaac75a0b56d1306aa59d0b05bbed7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen20201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20202" type="x-p"/> They shall never see light - Rise again they shall; but they shall never see the light of glory, for there is prepared for them the blackness of darkness for ever.
entries.1eb88367205ca0150e2d557ed3565ec362b38ec5: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen20202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20203" type="x-p"/> Man that is in honor - The rich and honorable man who has no spiritual understanding, is a beast in the sight of God. The spirit of this maxim is, A man who is in a dignified official situation, but destitute of learning and sound sense, is like a beast. The important place which he occupies reflects no honor upon him, but is disgraced by him. Who has not read the fable of the beautifully carved head? It was every thing that it should be, but had no brains. <div eID="gen20203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20204" type="x-p"/> This verse has been often quoted as a proof of the fall of man; and from ילין yalin, (in <reference osisRef="Psa.49.12">Psa 49:12</reference>), which signifies to lodge for a night, it has been inferred that Adam fell on the same day on which he was created, and that he did not spend a single night in the terrestrial paradise. Adam, who was in a state of glory, did not remain in it one night, but became stupid and ignorant as the beasts which perish. But we may rest assured this is no meaning of the text.  <chapter eID="Ps.49"/> <div eID="gen20204" type="x-p"/>

entries.be625c0f658d67cd0b75e37e044ee143140c80ea: <div eID="gen9498" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Of the Vanity of Earthly Prosperity and Good: A Didactic Poem</title> <div sID="gen9499" type="x-p"/> To the pair of <reference osisRef="Ps.47.1-Ps.47.9">Psa 47:1-9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.48.1-Ps.48.14">Psa 48:1-14</reference> is appended Psalms 49, which likewise begins with an appealing “all ye peoples;” in other respects, being a didactic song, it has nothing in common with the national and historical Psalms, Psa 46:1. The poet here steps forward as a preacher in the midst of men. His theme is the transitoriness of the prosperity of the ungodly, and, on the other hand, the hope of the upright which rests on God. Accordingly the Psalm falls into the following divisions: an introduction, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.2">Psa 49:2</reference>, which by its very promissory tone reminds one of the speeches of Elihu in the Book of Job, and the two parts of the sermon following thereupon, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.6">Psa 49:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Psa 49:14</reference>, which are marked out by a refrain, in which there is only a slight variation of expression. In its dogmatic character it harmonizes with the Psalms of the time of David, and by its antique and bold form takes rank with such Psalms as <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1-Ps.17.15">Psa 17:1-15</reference> by David and Ps 83 by Asaph. Since also in the didactic Psalms of David and Asaph we meet with a style differing from that of their other Psalms, and, where the doings of the ungodly are severely rebuked, we find a harsher and more concise mode of expression and a duller, heavier tone, there is nothing at variance with the assumption that Ps 49 was composed by the writer of <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1">Psa 42:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.84.1">Psa 84:1</reference>; and more especially since David has composed Psalms of a kindred character (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.1-Ps.39.13">Psa 39:1-13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.62.1-Ps.62.12">Psa 62:1-12</reference>) in the time of the persecution by Absalom. Nothing, however, is involved in this unity of the author. <div eID="gen9499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9500" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.1-Ps.49.4">Psa 49:1-4</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_49:2-5) Introduction. Very similarly do the elder (in the reign of Jehoshaphat) and the younger Micha (Micah) introduce their prophecies (1Ki 22:28; Mic 1:2); and Elihu in the Book of Job his didactic discourses (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.2">Psa 34:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.33.2">Psa 33:2</reference>). It is an universal theme which the poet intends to take up, hence he calls upon all peoples and all the inhabitants of the חלד. Such is the word first of all for this temporal life, which glides by unnoticed, them for the present transitory world itself (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Psa 17:14</reference>). It is his intention to declare to the rich the utter nothingness or vanity of their false ground of hope, and to the poor the superiority of their true ground of hope; hence he wishes to have as hearers both בני אדם, children of the common people, who are men and have otherwise nothing distinctive about them, and בּני־אישׁ, children of men, i.e., of rank and distinction (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>) - rich and poor, as he adds to make his meaning more clear. For his mouth will, or shall, utter הכמות, not: all sorts of wise teachings, but: weighty wisdom. Just in like manner תּבוּנות signifies profound insight or understanding; cf. plurals like בּינות, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.11">Isa 27:11</reference>, ישּׁוּעת, Ps. 42:12 and frequently, שׁלוּת, Jer 22:21. The parallel word תּבוּנות in the passage before us, and the plural predicate in <reference osisRef="Prov.24.7">Pro 24:7</reference>, show that חכמות, here and in <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Pro 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">Pro 9:1</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>, is not to be regarded, with Hitzig, Olshausen, and others, as another form of the singular חכמוּת. Side by side with the speaking of the mouth stands חגוּת לב (with an unchangeable <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> before the tone-syllable, Ew. §166, <hi type="italic">c</hi>): the meditation (lxx μελέτη) of the heart, and in accordance therewith the well-thought-out discourse. What he intends to discourse is, however, not the creation of his own brain, but what he has received. A משׁל, a saying embodying the wisdom of practical life, as God teaches men it, presents itself to his mind demanding to be heard; and to this he inclines his ear in order that, from being a diligent scholar of the wisdom from above, he may become a useful teacher of men, inasmuch as he opens up, i.e., unravels, the divine <hi type="italic">Mashal</hi>, which in the depth and fulness of its contents is a חידה, i.e., an involved riddle (from חוּד, cogn. אגד, עקד), and plays the cithern thereby (ב of the accompaniment). The opening of the riddle does not consist in the solving of it, but in the setting of it forth. פּתח, to open = to propound, deliver of a discourse, comes from the phrase את־ּפּיו-פּתח, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.26">Pro 31:26</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.130">Psa 119:130</reference>, where פּתח, an opening, is equivalent to an unlocking, a revelation.
entries.9e21906431205a2e551fd7104d7fee5260d9c4c7: <reference osisRef="Ps.49.5-Ps.49.12">Psa 49:5-12</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_49:6-13) First division of the sermon. Those who have to endure suffering from rich sinners have no need to fear, for the might and splendour of their oppressors is hastening towards destruction. ימי רע are days in which one experiences evil, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.13">Psa 94:13</reference>, cf. Amo 6:3. The genitive r` is continued in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Amo 6:6</reference></hi> in a clause that is subordinate to the בימי of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.49.6">Psa 49:6</reference></hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.15">1Sa 25:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.2">Job 29:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.15">Psa 90:15</reference>). The poet calls his crafty and malicious foes עקבי. There is no necessity for reading עקבי as Böttcher does, since without doubt a participial noun עקב, <hi type="italic">supplantator</hi>, can be formed from עקב, <hi type="italic">supplantare</hi>; and although in its branchings out it coincides with עקב, <hi type="italic">planta</hi>, its meaning is made secure by the connection. To render the passage: “when wickedness surrounds me about my heels,” whether with or without changing עון into עון (Hupfeld, von Ortenberg), is proved on all sides to be inadmissible: it ought to have been עול instead of עון; but even then it would still be an awkward expression, “to <hi type="italic">surround</hi> any one’s heels,”<note placement="foot">This might be avoided if it were possible for עון עקבי to mean “the sin that follows my heels, that follows me at the heels;” but apart from עון being unsuitable with this interpretation, an impossible meaning is thereby extorted from the genitive construction. This, however, is perhaps what is meant by the expression of the lxx, ἡ ἀνομία τῆς πτέρνης μου, so much spoken of in the Greek Church down to the present day.</note> and the הבּטחים, which follows, would be unconnected with what precedes. This last word comes after עקבי, giving minuteness to the description, and is then continued quite regularly in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.49.7">Psa 49:7</reference></hi> by the finite verb. Up to this point all is clear enough; but now the difficulties accumulate. One naturally expects the thought, that the rich man is not able to redeem himself from death. Instead of this it is said, that no man is able to redeem another from death. Ewald, Böttcher, and others, therefore, take אח, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.10">Eze 18:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.20">Eze 21:20</reference> (vid., Hitzig), to be a careless form of writing for אך, and change יפדּה into the reflexive יפּדה; but the thought that is sought thus to be brought to is only then arrived at with great difficulty: the words ought to be אך אישׁ לא יפדּה נפשׁו. The words as they stand assert: a brother (אח, as a prominently placed object, with <hi type="italic">Rebia magnum</hi>, = אהיו, cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">Eze 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.18">Eze 18:18</reference>; Mic 7:6; Mal 1:6) can a man by no means redeem, i.e., men cannot redeem one another. Hengstenberg and Hitzig find the thought that is to be expected in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.49.8">Psa 49:8</reference></hi>: the rich ungodly man can with all his riches not even redeem another (אח), much less then can he redeem himself, offer a כּפר for himself. But if the poet meant to be so understood, he must have written ולא and כּפר נפשׁו. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.49.8">Psa 49:8</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.49.8">Psa 49:8</reference></hi> bear no appearance of referring to different persons; the second clause is, on the contrary, the necessary supplement of the first: Among men certainly it is possible under some circumstances for one who is delivered over to death to be freed by money, but no כּפר (= פּדיון נפשׁ, <reference osisRef="Exod.21.30">Exo 21:30</reference> and frequently) can be given to God (לאלהים). <div eID="gen9500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9501" type="x-p"/> All idea of the thought one would most naturally look for must therefore be given up, so far as it can be made clear why the poet has given no direct expression to it. And this can be done. The thought of a man’s redeeming himself is far from the poet’s mind; and the contrast which he has before his mind is this: no man can redeem another, Elohim only can redeem man. That one of his fellow-men cannot redeem a man, is expressed as strongly as possible by the words לא־פדה יפדּה; the negative in other instances stands after the intensive infinitive, but here, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.4">Gen 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.8">Amo 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.28">Isa 28:28</reference>, before it. By an easy flight of irony, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.9">Psa 49:9</reference> says that the lu'tron which is required to be paid for the souls of men is too precious, i.e., exorbitant, or such as cannot be found, and that he (whoever might wish to lay it down) lets it alone (is obliged to let it alone) for ever  Thus much is clear enough, so far as the language is concerned (וחדל according to the <hi type="italic">consec. temp</hi>. = ויחדּל), and, although somewhat fully expressed, is perfectly in accordance with the connection. But how is <reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">Psa 49:10</reference> attached to what precedes? Hengstenberg renders it, “he must for ever give it up, that he should live continually and not see the grave.” But according to the syntax, ויהי cannot be attached to וחדל, but only to the futures in <reference osisRef="Ps.49.8">Psa 49:8</reference>, ranking with which the voluntative ויחי, <hi type="italic">ut vivat</hi> (Ew. §347, <hi type="italic">a</hi>). Thus, therefore, nothing remains but to take <reference osisRef="Ps.49.9">Psa 49:9</reference> (which von Ortenberg expunges as a gloss upon <reference osisRef="Ps.49.8">Psa 49:8</reference>) as a parenthesis; the principal clause affirms that no man can give to God a ransom that shall protect another against death, so that this other should still continue (עוד) to live, and that without end (לנצח), without seeing the grave, i.e., without being obliged to go down into the grave. The כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">Psa 49:11</reference> is now confirmatory of what is denied by its opposite; it is, therefore, according to the sense, <hi type="italic">imo</hi> (cf. 1Ki 21:15): ...that he may not see the grave - no indeed, without being able to interpose and alter it, he must see how all men, without distinction, succumb to death. Designedly the word used of the death of wise men is מוּת, and of the death of the fool and the stupid man, אבד. Kurtz renders: “together with the fool and the slow of understanding;”; but יחד as a proposition cannot be supported; moreover, ועזבוּ would then have “the wise” as its subject, which is surely not the intention of the poet. Everything without distinction, and in mingled confusion, falls a prey to death; the rich man must see it, and yet he is at the same time possessed by the foolish delusion that he, with his wealth, is immortal. <div eID="gen9501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9502" type="x-p"/> The reading קברם (lxx, Targ., Syr.), preferred by Ewald, and the conjecture קברם, adopted by Olshausen and Riehm, give a thought that is not altogether contrary to the connection, viz., the narrow grave is the eternal habitation of those who called broad lands their own; but this thought appears here, in view of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.49.12">Psa 49:12</reference></hi>, too early. קרב denotes the inward part, or that which is within, described according to that which encircles or contains it: that which is within them is, “their houses (pronounce <hi type="italic">bāttēmo</hi>) are for ever” (Hengstenberg, Hitzig); i.e., the contents of their inward part is the self-delusion that their houses are everlasting, and their habitations so durable that one generation after another will pass over them; cf. the similar style of expression in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference></hi>, Est 5:7. Hitzig further renders: men celebrate their names in the lands; קרא בשׁם, to call with a name = solemnly to proclaim it, to mention any one’s name with honour (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa 44:5</reference>). But it is unlikely that the subject of קראוּ should now again be any other than the rich men themselves; and עלי אדמות for בּכל־הארץ or בּארצות is contrary to the usage of the language. אדמה is the earth as tillage, אדמות (only in this passage) in this connection, fields, estates, lands; the proclaiming of names is, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.28">2Sa 12:28</reference>; 1Ki 8:43; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.12">Amo 9:12</reference>, equivalent to the calling of the lands or estates after their (the possessors') names (Böttcher, Hupfeld, Kurtz). The idea of the rich is, their houses and dwelling-places (and they themselves who have grown up together with them) are of eternal duration; accordingly they solemnly give their own names to their lands, as being the names of immortals. But, adds the poet, man בּיקר, in the pomp of his riches and outward show, abideth not (<hi type="italic">non pernoctat</hi> = <hi type="italic">non permanet</hi>). ביקר is the complement of the subject, although it logically (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>) also belongs to בּל־ילין. Böttcher has shown the impropriety of reading בּל־יבין here according to Psa 49:20. There are other instances also of refrains that are not exact repetitions; and this correction is moreover at once overthrown by the fact that בל will not suit יבין, it would stamp each man of rank, as such, as one deficient in intelligence. On the other hand, this emotional negative בל is admirably suitable to ילין: no indeed, he has no abiding. He is compared (נמשׁל like the New Testament ὡμοιώθη), of like kind and lot, to cattle (כּ as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.19">Job 30:19</reference>). נדמוּ is an attributive clause to כּבּהמות: like heads of cattle which are cut off or destroyed. The verb is so chosen that it is appropriate at the same time to men who are likened to the beasts (Hos 10:7, Hos 10:15, Oba 1:5, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.5">Isa 6:5</reference>).
entries.31e42afc2709f0c30a2c89222030f6605ad3f6d2: <reference osisRef="Ps.49.13-Ps.49.20">Psa 49:13-20</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_49:14-21) Second part of the discourse, of equal compass with the first. Those who are thought to be immortal are laid low in Hades; whilst, on the other hand, those who cleave to God can hope to be redeemed by Him out of Hades. Olshausen complains on this passage that the expression is abrupt, rugged, and in part altogether obscure. The fault, however, lies not, as he thinks, in a serious corruption of the text, but in the style, designedly adopted, of Psalms like this of a gloomy turn. זה דרכּם refers back to <reference osisRef="Ps.49.13">Psa 49:13</reference>, which is the proper <hi type="italic">mashal</hi> of the Psalm: this is their way or walk (דּרך as in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.5">Psa 37:5</reference>, cf. Hag 1:5). Close upon this follows כּסל למו (their way), of those (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">Psa 69:4</reference>) who possess self-confidence; כּסל signifies confidence both in a good and bad sense, self-confidence, impudence, and even (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.25">Ecc 7:25</reference>) in general, folly. The attributive clause is continued in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Psa 49:14</reference></hi>: and of those who after them (i.e., when they have spoken, as Hitzig takes it), or in a more universal sense: after or behind them (i.e., treading in their footsteps), have pleasure in their mouth, i.e., their haughty, insolent, rash words (cf. Jdg 9:38). If the meaning were “and after them go those who,” etc., then one would expect to find a verb in connection with אחריהם (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.21.33">Job 21:33</reference>). As a collateral definition, “after them = after their death,” it would, however, without any reason, exclude the idea of the assent given by their contemporaries. It is therefore to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Job.29.22">Job 29:22</reference>, or more universally according to Deu 12:30. It may seem remarkable that the music here strikes in <hi type="italic">forte</hi>; but music can on its part, in mournfully shrill tones, also bewail the folly of the world. <div eID="gen9502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9503" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Psa 49:14</reference>, so full of eschatological meaning, now describes what becomes of the departed. The subject of שׁתּוּ (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.73.9">Psa 73:9</reference>, where it is <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, for שׁתוּ) is not, as perhaps in the case of ἀπαιτοῦσιν, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luk 12:20</reference>, higher powers that are not named; but שׁוּת (here שׁתת), as in <reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Psa 3:7</reference>, Hos 6:11; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.7">Isa 22:7</reference>, is used in a semi-passive sense: like a herd of sheep they lay themselves down or they are made to lie down לשׁאול (thus it is pointed by Ben-Asher; whereas Ben-Naphtali points לשׁאול, with a silent <hi type="italic">Shebâ</hi>), to Hades = down into Hades (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.88.7">Psa 88:7</reference>), so that they are shut up in it like sheep in their fold. And who is the shepherd there who rules these sheep with his rod? מות ירעם. Not the good Shepherd (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.1">Psa 23:1</reference>), whose pasture is the land of the living, but Death, into whose power they have fallen irrecoverably, shall pasture them. Death is personified, as in <reference osisRef="Job.18.14">Job 18:14</reference>, as the king of terrors. The <hi type="italic">modus consecutivus</hi>, ויּרדּוּ, now expresses the fact that will be realized in the future, which is the reverse side of that other fact. After the night of affliction has swiftly passed away, there breaks forth, for the upright, a morning; and in this morning they find themselves to be lords over these their oppressors, like conquerors, who put their feet upon the necks of the vanquished (the lxx well renders it by κατακυριεύσουσιν).
